extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, philosophers of mathematics, and advanced students interested in foundations and mathematical practice
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging mathematical proofs, conjectures, and heuristic evidence, contrasting real mathematical practice with formal/metamathematical models. Emphasizes how proofs are accepted, what counts as understanding, and the limits of formal or probabilistic justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal derivations are infallible in principle (metamathematics)
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal derivation in first-order logic (metamathematics) portrays a structure of proofs which are indeed infallible 'in principle.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such derivations are hypothetical activities (except for 'toy' problems). They allow study of consequences of imagined infallible proofs and variations (e.g., constructivist rule changes), but this infallibility belongs to the model, not to everyday mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real proofs are socially established by qualified consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: Real mathematics has proofs which are established by 'consensus of the qualified.' A real proof is not checkable by a machine, or even by any mathematician not privy to the gestalt, the mode of thought of the particular field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences of opinion about completeness or correctness are resolved by communication and explanation, never by transcribing the proof into first-order predicate calculus. Acceptance is social and communicative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete informal proof criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: In real mathematical practice we distinguish a complete (informal) proof as one in which every step in the argument is convincing to the intended reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As formal proofs, both complete and incomplete informal proofs may be incomplete; thus 'complete informal proof' is a normative standard relative to an intended audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rock-bottom status for theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: A theorem comes to be regarded as 'rock bottom' when it is widely known and used, its proof frequently studied, alternative proofs are invented, it has known applications and generalizations, and is analogous to known results in related areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This accumulation of usage and interconnection is the practical basis for regarding foundational results (e.g., arithmetic, Euclidean geometry) as secure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model vs practice: caution about identifying mathematics with its formal model
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an error to identify mathematics itself with its model or representation in metamathematics (first-order logic). The presence of an infallible notion of proof in the model does not eliminate fallibility in real proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One must distinguish normative claims ('mathematics should be like a formal system') from descriptive claims ('mathematics is like a formal system'), and beware of rhetorical overreach in logic texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of formal logic as a tool, not a justificatory shortcut
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic offers theories which can serve as tools for analysts or algebraists (e.g., nonstandard analysis), but this has no relation to justifying proofs by translating them into formulas of first‑order logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logical results can be interesting and yield nontrivial theorems (e.g., relative strength results), but their significance for everyday mathematical truth is a matter of individual judgment and accumulated favorable judgment by many individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic evidence (bold conjecture + tests) strengthens belief but is not proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristic methods—formulating a bold conjecture and subjecting it to numerical calculation or other tests—can greatly strengthen conviction in a conjecture though they do not constitute deductive proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such evidence is analogous to scientific confirmation: failure to refute through tests increases confidence but cannot substitute for a proof; still it often suffices for working mathematicians to act as if true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of probabilistic/random models for deterministic sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating deterministic arithmetic functions (e.g., the Möbius function) 'as if they were random variables' can provide a 'good reason' for believing conjectures (e.g., Riemann hypothesis) by probabilistic arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach hinges on the feeling that the sequence 'looks' chaotic; numerical support (statistical agreement) strengthens the model, but the methodology replaces a deterministic question by a probabilistic one and so carries conceptual caveats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical confirmation is suggestive but not conclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: Very close numerical agreement between calculation and heuristic prediction (even to many decimal places) is compelling and unlikely to be accidental, but history shows that behavior verified up to huge bounds can still fail eventually (Littlewood example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerical evidence may justify strong belief (realist/Platonist stance) but cannot establish mathematical truth in the deductive sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof as understanding: perspicuity matters
rubrics_metrics.description: We want a proof because a proof is a way of understanding why a conjecture is true; a proof that is so complex and non-perspicuous that it sheds no light fails to serve this purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perspicuous (illuminating) proofs are valued; a 500-page proof that cannot be followed may confirm truth technically but provide little understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of a long/complex proof depends on expert judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: If a long and arduous proof is published, its correctness will be decided by a sufficient number of experts; even then, detection of errors may take generations and acceptance remains a social process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex proofs require community vetting; expertise and the 'gestalt' of the field determine whether steps are convincing to intended readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructivist criterion: existence = constructibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructivists hold that a mathematical object's existence is only meaningful when there is a constructive procedure to produce it; certain classical logical principles (e.g., law of excluded middle) do not apply to statements about infinite expansions unless a construction is known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This leads to alternative standards for truth: a statement like 'either P or not P' may be rejected in absence of a constructive proof of either, and the definition of reals is tied to algorithms for decimal expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of real numbers by computation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A real number can be defined by a definite calculating procedure (algorithm) which gives the decimal expansion to as many terms as desired; the 'existence' of further digits beyond those computed is not assumed by constructivists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This operational notion underpins constructivist objections to classical principles and affects whether certain comparisons (e.g., law of trichotomy) are accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of formal systems for explaining mathematical development
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal systems fail to give a direct account of the historical growth of mathematics or the day-to-day experience of practitioners; other explanatory principles (e.g., drive toward unification) may better explain development in some fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatos' picture (mathematics living and growing via proofs and refutations) is offered as an alternative corrective to the formal-systems model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic testing methodology: boldness, specificity, and falsifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: A good heuristic conjecture should be bold, very precise and informative (not likely true by accident), and subjected to tests (numerical experiments) that could potentially refute it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mirrors Popperian scientific methodology applied to mathematical conjectures: the more informative (risky) a conjecture, the more its survival of tests should increase confidence in it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of alternative proofs and applications in increasing confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention of alternative proofs, known applications, generalizations, and analogies to related areas provide independent confirmations that increase trust in a result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These multiple lines of support are part of what makes a result 'rock bottom' and reduce the probability that an accepted proof contains serious undetected errors.
